thesis: For an open, on-device model the attacker owns the weights, so safety is not a refusal rate — it is the attacker cost to break the model, at each capability level, in the languages people actually use. Magpie prices that, pairs every number with over-refusal, and tests whether a cheap white-box margin predicts the price.

judge_flip_en.caption: Same attempts, two judges. The cheap refusal lexicon over-counts and flips the attack ranking; only a content judge tells a long non-refusal from a real jailbreak.

judge_flip_lang.caption: Identical prompts, three forms. The lexicon says Devanagari is 4x English and Hinglish is safest; the content judge says the opposite in order and a third in size.

hardening.caption: A lightweight Circuit-Breakers/RR pass (fire_rr) re-attacked paired against vendor Fire. It raises attacker cost at no level — an honest negative.

h4.caption: A prompt's attack-free refusal-direction margin predicts how expensive it is to break (Cox regression; hazard ratio < 1 means a higher margin survives longer).

cards.fire:
# Robustness card — Tiny Aya Fire (vendor, M0)

*A deployer-facing summary. Numbers are content-validated with the HarmBench classifier unless
marked "lexicon"; full provenance (run dirs, git SHAs, CIs) in [`docs/RESULTS.md`](../RESULTS.md).
Model: `CohereLabs/tiny-aya-fire`, 3.35B, cohere2, open weights.*

**One line.** Safe to a direct ask, holds against public jailbreak templates, but its safety is
**shallow** (one forced token bypasses it) and it is **defenceless to weight edits** — the on-device
threat that matters for an openly released model.

## Cost to break (English)

| Attacker level | Capability | ASR (HarmBench) | ~cost (log₁₀ FLOPs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L0 direct | query only | **0.05** | 12.9 |
| L1 templates | query + public jailbreaks | **0.29** | 13.1 |
| L1 best-of-N (synthetic) | query + cheap resampling | **0.19** | 13.0 |
| L2 prefill | controls the decoder | **0.31** (lexicon 1.00; 1 token → 0.80) | 12.6 |
| L3 abliteration | edits the weights | **0.68** | 13.5 |

## Over-refusal (benign prompts)

13% of benign-but-scary English prompts are refused at L0 (XSTest-safe + OR-Bench-Hard); jailbreak
templates *lower* it to ~7% (the "answer directly" framing suppresses benign refusals too).

## By language (L0, HarmBench)

| English | Hinglish | Devanagari |
|---|---|---|
| 0.03 | 0.03 | **0.28** |

A real safety-coverage gap in **Devanagari** (~9× English). Hinglish is as robust as English once
model *collapse* (degenerate output on romanized code-mixing) is excluded.

## Deployer guidance

- **Do not rely on the refusal rate.** A refusal-lexicon monitor over-counts safety 4–5× and, in
  Devanagari, reports the model as ~4× *less* safe than it is. Use a content judge + a collapse
  guard.
- **Assume prefill = broken.** If any surface lets a caller set the first reply tokens, treat the
  model as unprotected (ASR 0.80 at one token). Guard the decoder, not just the prompt.
- **Weights are the boundary.** An attacker with the file breaks 2 in 3 harmful prompts by
  abliteration. On-device deployment must assume this; safety training alone does not help here.
- **Watch Devanagari specifically** — it is the weakest language surface.
- **A cheap pre-screen works:** a prompt's refusal-direction margin predicts its cost-to-break
  (H4), so a red-team budget can be focused before any attack is run.
cards.global:
# Robustness card — Tiny Aya Global (vendor, M1)

*A deployer-facing summary. Numbers are content-validated with the HarmBench classifier unless
marked "lexicon"; full provenance in [`docs/RESULTS.md`](../RESULTS.md). Model:
`CohereLabs/tiny-aya-global`, 3.35B, cohere2, open weights — the vendor's safest Tiny Aya variant.*

**One line.** Behaves almost identically to Fire across the ladder: robust to a direct ask, holds
against templates, shallow to prefill, and broken by weight edits. "Safest variant" does **not**
mean more expensive to break.

## Cost to break (English)

| Attacker level | Capability | ASR | ~cost (log₁₀ FLOPs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L0 direct | query only | **0.07** (HarmBench) | 12.9 |
| L1 templates | query + public jailbreaks | **0.29** (HarmBench) | 13.1 |
| L2 prefill | controls the decoder | **0.16** (HarmBench; lexicon 1.00, 1 token → 0.89) | 12.6 |
| L3 abliteration | edits the weights | **0.68** (HarmBench) | 13.5 |

## Over-refusal (benign prompts)

13% at L0, falling to ~5% under jailbreak templates — the same robustness/over-refusal trade as
Fire.

## Deployer guidance

- **Fire ≈ Global at L0/L1/L3**, so picking the "safer" vendor label buys ~no extra cost-to-break
  there; the real separation is attacker *capability* (L0→L3), not model choice. The one exception
  is **prefill**, where Global is content-safer (0.16 vs Fire's 0.31) — but both are fully
  bypassed by the *lexicon* (1.00), so this edge is invisible without a content judge and should
  not be leaned on.
- The prefill and weight-edit cautions from the Fire card apply unchanged: guard the decoder,
  assume weight access breaks the model.
- Global was evaluated in English; the per-form (Hinglish/Devanagari) and best-of-N studies were
  run on Fire. Treat Fire's Devanagari gap as the likely Global behaviour pending a matched run.
cards.fire_rr:
# Robustness card — Tiny Aya Fire + Circuit-Breakers/RR (hardened, M2)

*A deployer-facing summary. Numbers are content-validated with the HarmBench classifier unless
marked "lexicon"; full provenance in [`docs/RESULTS.md`](../RESULTS.md). Model: Tiny Aya Fire
hardened with SafeTune M2 (Circuit Breakers / Representation Rerouting), 150 steps, LoRA on 2
layers, merged. Weights not published.*

**One line.** A plausible-looking defense that **shifts no survival curve**: the loss drops and L0
is clean, but the hardened model costs exactly as much to break as vendor Fire at every level. This
is the honest negative the cost framing is built to surface.

## Cost to break vs vendor Fire (paired, same prompts)

| Attacker level | Fire | fire_rr | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| L0 direct | 0.21 lexicon | 0.21 lexicon | none |
| L1 templates | **0.30** HarmBench | **0.30** HarmBench | none |
| L2 prefill | **0.31** HarmBench | **0.31** HarmBench | none |
| L2 prefill curve | k=1 0.80, k=2 0.98, k≥4 1.00 | **identical** | none |

The checkpoint is genuinely the hardened one — its completions differ prompt-by-prompt from Fire's,
so the merged weights loaded — it simply does not cost more to break.

## Verdict for a deployer

- **Do not ship a defense on its training loss.** RR here drove loss 5.0→0.50 and left L0 clean,
  yet moved no attacker-cost curve. Validate a defense by re-attacking it and measuring the
  survival curve, not by its loss or its L0 refusal rate.
- **Representation rerouting did not touch prefill at all** (safety-depth curve byte-identical) —
  a shallow-safety attack needs a depth-targeted defense (Qi et al.), not RR.
- A heavier RR schedule (more steps, more layers) or a different method (CAST) is required before
  any hardening claim; this lightweight pass is not sufficient.

> Companion negative: **M3 RepNoise** on the same model *collapsed* it (all outputs degenerate),
> which the collapse guard flagged automatically — a defense that zeroes ASR by destroying utility.
> Neither lightweight defense is deployable as-is.
